This record therefore documents the conflict instead of transferring Maxon specifications onto the DOD entry.

The available evidence consistently associates **D&S Distortion & Sustainer** and **D&S II Distortion & Sustainer II** with **Maxon**, not DOD.

Effects Database identifies the **Maxon OD-802 D&S II** as a Maxon 808-series distortion/sustain pedal and dates the D&S II to **1974**. Maxon's own current reissue product page calls the model **DISTORTION AND SUSTAINER II (D&S II)** and identifies it as a Maxon pedal. [1][2]

A separate manual for the D&S II identifies controls for **Distortion, Tone, and Balance**, plus Normal/Effect switching and 9V battery/adapter operation. The same manual identifies the pedal as D&S II Distortion & Sustainer II. [3]

Searches for an exact DOD-branded D&S or D&S II pedal did not produce comparable first-party DOD documentation. The current DigiTech/DOD product-manual index includes many DOD products but did not surface a DOD D&S/D&S II manual in the reviewed results. [4]

Because the archive record currently says DOD Electronics, the following information is **evidence about the Maxon model family only** and should not be rendered on this DOD entry as settled DOD data until the catalog identity is corrected or independently corroborated.

- **Manufacturer:** Maxon
- **Model:** D&S II / OD-802
- **Catalog family:** Maxon 808 series
- **Type:** Distortion / sustainer
- **Controls:** Distortion, Tone, Balance
- **Circuit description:** Maxon describes a dual-op-amp design related to the OD808, with increased low-end, output, and gain. [1][2]
- **Current draw:** Maxon's reissue specification lists 6 mA at 9V battery operation and 7 mA at 10V adapter operation. [2]
- **Power:** 9V battery or special AC adapter; Maxon's reissue specification lists DC9V battery operation and DC10V adapter operation. [2]
- **Dimensions:** 61 mm × 112 mm × 35 mm main body; 70 mm × 112 mm × 55 mm overall in the current Maxon reissue specification. [2]
- **Weight:** 260 g in Maxon's current reissue specification. [2]

Historical/technical sources further describe the D&S II as using a diode-clipping stage and a tone circuit with added low-frequency control; some secondary sources identify germanium clipping and different op-amp implementations across vintage examples. Those component claims vary by version and source, so they should not be normalized into one universal D&S II circuit without a specific unit or schematic. [1][5][6]

Maxon Maxon 808 series browse by type distortion/fuzz/overdrive distortion browse by type volume/amplification sustain browse by enclosure pedal Maxon OD-802 D & S II Distortion/Sustainer Published on August 7, 2005 Maxon 808 series distortion sustain pedal original original original original reissue reissue Controls Distortion controls the amount of distortion Tone controls the tone (bass/treble?) Level/Balance controls the mix of the input signal with the distorted signal Information Maxon USA Originally released in 1974, the D&S II Distortion & Sustainer II is a precursor to the amp-overdrive simulators of later years. With its mild drive, relaxed sustain and high output, the D&S II sits the fence between an overdrive and a distortion. This unique "split personality" makes the D&S II perfect for players that seek a natural-feeling drive sound but with more drive and output than an OD generally provides. The D&S II accomplishes this task with some unique circuit refinements not typically found in distortions. Like a standard distortion, the D&S II features a diode-clipping stage after the amplifier section of the circuit. However, rather than using the silicon diodes commonly found in today's circuits, the D&S II uses germanium diodes in this clipping stage. The threshold voltage for clipping is 0.1 - 0.2V with germanium and 0.7 - 0.8V with silicon, so the germanium can distort even low level tones, thus making a smoother distortion. In addition, the germanium's rectifier characteristic is inferior to silicon (voltage drop with negative current is not as sharp as that of silicon) - this shortcoming ironically works favorably for the D&S II, creating a somewhat rounded waveform of the clipped signal that contributes to the unit's warm, natural distortion. Due to their "inferior" characteristics, germanium diodes are now a very rare component and have generally been replaced with silicon diodes in other manufacturer's circuits. Ironically, it is these shortcomings that give the D&S II its signature sound. Also unique to the D&S II is its tone control. While most other overdrives and distortions feature hi boost/hi cut tone circuits, the D&S II tone control uses a low range boost/cut circuit for added bottom end. In addition, the D&S II's tone circuit features the JRC4558 IC chip,
